entities.name: All-India Muslim League
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The All-India Muslim League (AIML), founded in 1906 in Dhaka under Nawab Khwaja Salimullah's patronage — gathering Muslim elites who feared the impact of the 1905 Bengal Partition reversal and Hindu-dominated Congress politics on Muslim interests — became under Muhammad Ali Jinnah's leadership (1934-1947) the principal vehicle for the demand for a separate Muslim state of Pakistan, achieving partition of British India and the creation of Pakistan on August 14, 1947 — one of the largest and most violent forced migrations in human history.

The League's transformation from a conservative Muslim elite organization to a mass nationalist movement demanding partition was largely Jinnah's achievement. Jinnah (initially a Congress member committed to Hindu-Muslim unity) grew increasingly convinced after the 1937 provincial elections — where Congress refused to include League in coalition governments — that Muslims required a separate state. The 1940 Lahore Resolution formally demanded Pakistan; the 1942-1947 period saw intensifying Congress-League conflict.

The 1947 partition produced enormous violence: estimates of deaths range from 200,000 to 2 million, and 10-20 million people were displaced in both directions across the new India-Pakistan border — the largest forced migration in history until then. The League's demand for Pakistan and its achievement fundamentally reshaped the Indian subcontinent and the British Empire's end. The AIML itself effectively dissolved into Pakistani national politics after 1947, with successor parties using the Muslim League name in both Pakistan and India.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The All-India Muslim League — achieving the creation of Pakistan through one of history's most violent and consequential partitions, displacing 10-20 million people, and permanently reshaping South Asia — is one of the most historically consequential political parties in the 20th century.
